author: Chloe Smith
title: Updated: Voters reject school referendum - NewsBreak
text:
By Chloe Smith ,
1 days ago
PRINCETON – Voters residing in the Princeton School District flocked to the polls on Thursday, Nov. 4 made their voices heard on the proposed $49.14 million building bond and $750,000-per-year capital projects levy.
After two years of research and preparation by the district, the referendum was rejected and voters said “no” to the proposal.
With both the Princeton and Baldwin precincts reporting, 1,983 voters cast a "no" vote — 58.5% — while 1,404 or 41.4% voted "yes".
“The voters have spoken. The election result is disappointing for the school district, given the immense amount of research and discussion that went into developing this plan over the past two plus years,” Superintendent Pat Devine said. “We will need to move forward knowing the current conditions of our outdated and undersized facilities at the high school are not going away any time soon. We’ll need to rely on our general fund to address these facility needs over time, which means fewer resources for other facility needs for our students and staff.”
A total of 3,387 people flocked to the polls to make their voices heard.
According to statistics from the Princeton School District, voters were split almost evenly between the two precincts at 1,497 voters at the Princeton Depot Museum polling location and 1,360 voters at the Baldwin City Hall location.
Absentee votes totaled 535 with 327 from Princeton and 208 from Baldwin.
Princeton voters cast 781 "yes" votes and 1,039 "no" votes while 623 Baldwin area voters were in favor and 944 were against, absentee votes included.
“We respect the decision of our voters, but there will be some difficult choices ahead. We will continue working to find solutions that reflect community input and support student learning,” Princeton School Board Chair Deb Ulm said.
The single-question ballot asked voters to consider a building bond that would replace and modernize Career and Technical Education (CTE) spaces, renovate outdated classrooms and science labs, address overcrowding and accessibility challenges, and update aging infrastructure.
Some other improvements include the replacement of the boiler system in the high school and the replacement of the Princeton Middle School roof.
The capital project levy, also known as a tech levy, would have provided funds for the district to be used for technology systems related to safety and security, classroom and building technology, digital curriculum, support and maintenance of software, software licenses, computers, technology infrastructure and network improvements, device replacement, and to pay the costs of technology related personnel and training.
If approved by voters, the building bond would have remained in place for 20 years and the tech levy would have been in effect for 10 years at an estimated $15 tax increase per month for an average-valued home — approximately $350,000 — in the district.
The Princeton School Board will canvas and finalize the official election results during a special meeting on Monday, Nov. 10 in the District Center Board Room at noon.
"Thank you to everyone who participated in this election," the Princeton School District wrote on its website. "Thank you for staying engaged throughout this process and for coming out to vote."
For more information, visit isd477.org/referendum or contact Superintendent Pat Devine at election@isd477.org.
